contract.provides: Two passive systems can have identical accessible scattering and total-loss flags but exchange target/parasitic sink labels, so even adaptive external control cannot infer the hidden sink from that interface. A passive one-port resonator can reduce total loss while a new target sink absorbs positive energy. The positive finite-power saturable-bucket theorem is stated for 0<a<b and requires (ab)^(1/3)(a^(1/3)+b^(1/3))<=1, along with fixed delivered target-plane power, full complex control, complete energy collection, a qualified single-pass homogeneous saturable absorber, acquired response and reset. Nonlinear bucket and iTRAN methods are strong incumbents; no new demonstrated capability or practical advantage follows.

# Scientific operation: optical focusing from a saturation-dependent loss bucket

15 October 2026, Australia/Brisbane. Independent continuing inventor: `scientific_operation`.

**Disposition: a narrow conditional measurement construction, not a demonstrated new capability. Novelty and practical advantage are UNKNOWN.** A total photon-loss flag can measure and help optimize total extinction. It cannot identify which internal sink received the energy. A temporary, specimen-specific nonlinear state can supply additional information, but only if its response is acquired and the readout isolates it. The strongest proposed mutation here is an energy-detector-only feedback measurement of a thin saturable absorber behind a static diffuser. The mathematical construction survives at two finite illumination powers. Its transfer to a useful physical specimen remains open.

The initial biological trapping scout was discontinued when the parent reassigned this worker to a non-biological instrumentation problem. No biological construction is promoted or incorporated here. This worker did not read the other current invention workers. One limited literature helper independently checked the exact optical overlap after this candidate was constructed; its report is in `literature_audit/REPORT.md`.

## 1. What is being proposed, and why it might matter

Send a controllable coherent wave through a static scattering layer to a thin, homogeneous saturable absorber. For each trial wavefront, illuminate at two known powers, retaining the launched-energy monitor and **all accessible outgoing energy**, including reflected and transmitted channels. Compute the difference between the two normalized missing-energy fractions. Use that one scalar to update the incident wavefront.

The temporary intermediate state is ground-state depletion in the absorber. It reduces the fractional absorption most strongly in bright speckles. Under the explicitly stated model below, the two-power loss deficit is a convex concentration functional: its maximum places the delivered power in one target-plane mode. The feedback detector does not have to image or recover the phase of that mode.

# Targeted literature audit: saturable-loss bucket feedback

## Finding

Closest papers establish both absorption-saturation focusing and focusing from scalar nonlinear buckets. I found no primary paper in this targeted search using the specific low/high-power, launched-power-normalized total-loss decrease of a homogeneous saturable absorber as the optimization bucket. This is a scoped observation, not a novelty claim.

## Exact overlaps

- **Absorption nonlinearity and an extended absorber layer:** Cui, Kahraman & Wang, “[Optical focusing into scattering media via iterative time reversal guided by absorption nonlinearity](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-025-63095-w),” *Nature Communications* 16, 7807 (2025), show speckle-scale focusing with ground-state-depletion eosin/gelatin between diffusers. Their feedback is **complex backscatter measured by four-step digital holography**: scaled low/high fields are subtracted and phase-conjugated. This establishes absorber focusing, not scalar total-loss feedback. Their apparatus uses an SLM, camera/reference path, AOMs and monitors; the loop takes about 14 s/iteration. Eosin saturation intensity is near 0.6 W cm⁻², with photobleaching and oxygen-quenching limits.
- **Scalar nonlinear bucket and focusing:** Katz, Small, Guan & Silberberg, “[Noninvasive nonlinear focusing and imaging through strongly scattering turbid layers](https://doi.org/10.1364/OPTICA.1.000170),” *Optica* 1, 170–174 (2014), maximize epi-detected total 2PF with one integrating detector and a genetic algorithm, without image feedback. A thin homogeneous fluorescent screen behind a diffuser forms a diffraction-limited focus; a second demonstration focuses through 1 mm brain tissue onto crystallites. This is scalar nonlinear-bucket focusing, with emitted 2PF rather than normalized absorption loss. For thick homogeneous 3D 2PF, total signal may be waist-independent, so target-plane geometry matters. The planar bucket rose only about 50% despite higher peak intensity.
- **General theory and scalar feedback test:** Osnabrugge, Amitonova & Vellekoop, “[Blind focusing through strongly scattering media using wavefront shaping with nonlinear feedback](https://doi.org/10.1364/OE.27.011673),” *Optics Express* 27, 11673–11688 (2019); [author-hosted full text](https://arxiv.org/html/1902.02718v1).
